extracted.intended_audience: labor-law practitioners, employers, unions, and regulators involved in joint-employer rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and legal review of the NLRB's final joint-employer rule under the NLRA, with particular focus on APA arbitrariness, Regulatory Flexibility Act compliance, and how various factors (control, essential terms) determine joint-employer status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer general-duty to furnish safe workplace
rubrics_metrics.description: An employer must furnish to each of his employees employment and a place of employment which are free from recognized hazards that are causing or are likely to cause death or serious physical harm to his employees; and shall comply with occupational safety and health standards promulgated under this chapter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This duty (OSHA general duty clause) is owed to an employer's own employees but subsection (a)(2) requires employers to implement safety standards for the benefit of all employees in a given workplace, even employees of another employer (Universal Construction Co. v. OSHRC). Thus compliance may require an employer to exert control over workplace health and safety of workers employed by other employers.

rubrics_metrics.name: OSHA multi-employer worksite employer categories and duties
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA guidance identifies four types of employers on a multi-employer worksite: the creating employer, the exposing employer, the correcting employer, and the controlling employer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creating employer: caused a hazardous condition that violates an OSHA standard. Exposing employer: whose own employees have been exposed. Correcting employer: engaged in a common undertaking and responsible for correcting the hazard. Controlling employer: has general supervisory authority over the worksite, including power to correct violations or require others to correct them. Each type owes duties to employees; extent of duties depends on categorization and an employer may have multiple roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlling employer responsibility to abate hazards (Universal Construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A controlling employer (e.g., a general contractor) is responsible for safety violations that it could reasonably have been expected to prevent or abate by reason of its supervisory capacity, regardless of whether it created the hazard or its own employees were exposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this precedent, exercising supervisory capacity to address hazards can create duties to abate even when the hazard originates with a subcontractor; the dissent argues the final joint-employer rule could convert such supervisory responses into joint-employer status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether 'working conditions related to the safety and health of employees' are an essential term
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule treats 'working conditions related to the safety and health of employees' as an essential term and condition of employment for joint-employer analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dissent argues this is at odds with OSHA guidance and that making safety-related working conditions 'essential' could produce cross-coverage of other employers' employees (and unintended joint-employer findings) whenever a business applies safety measures to all persons on its premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether 'work rules and directions governing manner, means, or methods and grounds for discipline' are essential terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule adds 'work rules and directions governing the manner, means, or methods of the performance of duties and the grounds for discipline' to the list of essential terms and conditions of employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dissent warns that the phrase, especially 'grounds for discipline,' invites unions to scrutinize user-employer manuals for ambiguous language that 'could' be interpreted to interfere with protected activity, enabling joint-employer findings even where the user employer never actually applied those rules to supplier employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether 'tenure of employment, including hiring and discharge' is an essential term
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule substitutes 'hiring' and 'discharge' with 'the tenure of employment, including hiring and discharge' as an essential term of employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dissent explains this could be used to argue general contractors indirectly control the duration of project-based hires (e.g., hiring-hall staff brought on for a subcontract) and thereby be treated as joint employers per se, expanding joint-employer liability in industries with project-based staffing practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA requirement of reasoned explanation and response to comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Administrative Procedure Act, an agency must provide a reasoned explanation for its action, show good reasons for a new policy, and respond to significant points raised in vital comments; agency action that is not reasonable and reasonably explained is arbitrary and capricious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities include FCC v. Fox Television Stations and FCC v. Prometheus; the dissent faults the final rule for failing adequately to respond to significant comments and for resting on a legally erroneous premise that common-law agency principles compel the Board's approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must justify that new rule provides clarity and reduces uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency claiming the final rule will provide 'a definite and readily available standard' and reduce uncertainty and litigation must demonstrate those benefits; bare assertions are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dissent finds the final rule does not, in practice, provide greater certainty than adjudication because it repeatedly incorporates the common law by reference and thus leaves most determinations to case-by-case adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation of common-law agency principles must provide guidance (not merely reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely incorporating the common law of agency by reference (e.g., sections stating determination is 'under common-law agency principles') without explaining how common-law principles will be applied does not provide meaningful regulatory guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections cited: 103.40(a), (e), (f). The dissent argues that reliance on the common law without explication effectively returns parties to case-by-case adjudication and fails the Board's obligation to provide a clear rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: FRFA statutory content requirements (Regulatory Flexibility Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Final Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (FRFA) must state the purpose of the final rule, estimate the number of small businesses affected (if possible), summarize comments filed in response to the IRFA along with the agency's assessment, and include a description of steps taken to minimize significant economic impacts and factual, policy, and legal reasons for choosing the adopted alternative and rejecting others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited statutory authority: 5 U.S.C. 601-612, 5 U.S.C. 604(a)(6). Failure to satisfy these requirements can render the rulemaking arbitrary and capricious for RFA purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of direct compliance costs on small entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the RFA, an agency must consider direct compliance costs imposed by the rule on small entities subject to the regulation; costs tied to obligations imposed by the rule (e.g., new bargaining duties) are direct costs that must be analyzed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dissent argues the Board erroneously treated many such costs as irrelevant or speculative—examples of direct costs include the obligation to determine joint-employer status by reviewing contracts/practices and the immediate duty to bargain (with attendant legal and negotiation costs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not ignore practical (non-speculative) consequences framed as 'voluntary'
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency cannot evade consideration of compliance costs merely because a provision is framed as 'voluntary' if its practical effect coerces compliance (e.g., to avoid liability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited case: AFL-CIO v. Chertoff; practical effect matters — safe-harbor or voluntary compliance that in practice compels action can impose significant costs on small entities and must be analyzed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable and realistic estimation of familiarization/compliance time and costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimates of the time and cost small businesses will spend reading and understanding a rule (and consulting counsel) must be realistic given the rule's length, complexity, and the likely lack of HR or legal staff at many small firms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dissent criticizes the majority's estimate of one hour to read ~63,000 words and one hour of counsel time as implausibly low and argues such underestimates render the FRFA arbitrary and capricious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate billing/wage rates when calculating legal consultation costs
rubrics_metrics.description: When estimating attorney consultation costs, agencies should use realistic billable rates (or otherwise justified rates) rather than relying on average wage statistics that substantially understate market billing rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dissent contrasts the BLS average wage the majority used with higher market billable rates (Clio report, Laffey Matrix) and argues counsel will often need far more than one hour to analyze impacts — both the rate and time should reflect real-world practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must explain why it replaces a clearer prior rule with a less-guiding standard
rubrics_metrics.description: When amending or rescinding a previous rule that provided specific factors and guidance (the 2020 Rule), an agency must give good reasons for replacing it with a rule that offers less specific guidance and returns determinations to the common law or adjudication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dissent emphasizes that the 2020 Rule enumerated specific factors that provided predictability; replacing it with a high-level incorporation of the common law reduces certainty and requires explanation and justification under the APA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude evidence of control over immaterial matters from joint-employer determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Per Section 103.40(f), evidence of an employer's control over matters immaterial to the existence of an employment relationship or matters that do not bear on employees' essential terms and conditions is 'not relevant' to joint-employer determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule text so provides, but the dissent contends that the Board mischaracterizes or misapplies common-law principles and that the rule nonetheless fails to meaningfully cabin what counts as 'immaterial' control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of jurisdictional effects (combining gross revenues) on small entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory analyses should account for effects on small businesses of ancillary procedural consequences the rule imposes, such as the Board's practice of combining gross revenues of joint employers for jurisdictional purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dissent notes that converting small firms into joint employers can import jurisdictional exposure (and attendant regulatory burdens), increasing the economic impact that must be considered in the FRFA.
